This robot doesn't move by walking. It grows. Developed by researchers at the Italian Institute of Technology, the robot extends itself by continuously 3D-printing a hollow thermoplastic tube from its tip. Instead of dragging its entire body through an environment, it creates new body length as it moves, allowing it to navigate spaces that would be nearly impossible for conventional robots. That's what makes the design so fascinating. Because the robot advances by growing rather than pushing or rolling, it can squeeze through narrow gaps, curve around obstacles, and explore confined environments without needing complex legs or wheels. The potential applications go far beyond the lab. Robots like this could one day assist in search-and-rescue missions, inspect damaged infrastructure, explore underground tunnels, or access hazardous areas that are too dangerous or inaccessible for people. It's also a reminder that robotics isn't only about building machines that imitate humans. Sometimes the most effective designs take inspiration from nature instead. Like climbing vines, this robot expands into its environment rather than forcing its way through it. The future of robotics may not always walk. Sometimes, it will simply grow. Gdansk, Poland ❤️🇵🇱⚓️ Located in northern Poland, on the shores of the Baltic Sea, Gdańsk has been shaped by its position as one of the most important trading cities in the region. Its historic centre is filled with beautifully reconstructed merchant houses, grand public buildings and Gothic churches, while the waterfront and former shipyard areas tell another important part of the city's story. ❤️🇵🇱 Some of Gdańsk's most recognisable landmarks include Długi Targ and the colourful Long Market, the Neptune Fountain, the Green Gate, St. Mary's Basilica, the historic Gdańsk Crane and the European Solidarity Centre. 🏛️⚓️✨ Walking through the city, you'll also discover the Motława River, historic Granary Island, charming side streets and waterfront views that give Gdańsk its unmistakable character. The city's architecture reflects centuries of changing influences, with Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Dutch-inspired buildings creating one of the most distinctive urban landscapes in Poland. Many of the historic buildings were destroyed during World War II, making the reconstruction of Gdańsk's Old Town an important part of the city's modern story. 📸 Beyond the major landmarks, Gdańsk's charm comes from simply wandering through its streets, following the waterfront, discovering smaller architectural details and watching everyday life unfold between historic façades. 🇵🇱✨ A city shaped by the sea, trade, history and resilience, with one of the most beautiful historic cityscapes on the Baltic coast. ❤️ #gdansk #gdanskpoland #gdańsk #gdansktravel #gdanskcity

Potato Soup (serves 3-4)🥣🥔 ingredients: -4 large russet potatoes  -one large yellow onion -a head of garlic  -1/2 cup nutrional yeast  -one box veggie broth -one block of tofu  -carrots (2 large carrots or half a bag of baby carrots) -chopped stalk of celery  -@LightLife Bacon (4-5 pieces) -seasonings: oregano, smoked paprika, black pepper, garlic powder -olive oil or butter -plant milk Directions:  Cook the bacon in a pot with a small amount of oil or butter, then remove, crumble, and set it aside (vegan bacon won’t produce as much grease as animal bacon). cook down the onion and celery in the bacon grease. Çeşm-i Nigar - a soup with a name as beautiful as its meaning✨ Çeşm-i Nigar means “eyes of the beloved” a poetic name for this traditional Ottoman soup. Once enjoyed as part of Ottoman cuisine, today I wanted to bring this beautiful piece of Ottoman history into my kitchen🧡 Ingredients * 1 onion * 1 tbsp flour * 1 cup red lentils * ½ Turkish tea glass (60 ml) olive oil * 1 teaspoon salt * 6 cups (1,200 ml) water For the milk and egg mix (terbiye) * 1 Turkish tea glass (125 ml) milk * 1 egg yolk * Juice of ½ lemon For the topping * 1 tablespoon butter * 1 teaspoon dried mint * 1 teaspoon red pepper flakes 1. Wash the lentils thoroughly and drain them. 2. Heat the olive oil in a pot and add the finely chopped onion. Sauté until the onion becomes soft and lightly golden. 3. Add the flour and continue cooking until you can smell the cooked flour (2-3 mins) Keep the heat moderate and stir continuously to prevent the flour from burning. 4. Add the washes lentils and stir. Then add the hot water and leave the soup to cook until the lentils become very soft and break down. 5. Meanwhile, prepare the egg and milk mixture by whisking together the milk, lemon juice, and egg yolk. The lemon juice and milk used should be at room temperature. 6. Once the lentils are completely soft, turn off the heat and blend the soup until smooth. 7. Take about one ladleful of the hot soup and slowly add it to the milk and egg mixture while whisking. This gently brings the mixture up to temperature and prevents the egg from curdling. 8. Slowly pour the warmed mixture into the soup while stirring continuously. 9. Turn the heat back on and let the soup simmer for a few minutes. Then add a bit of salt. 10. Give it one final stir and remove it from the heat. 11. For the topping, melt the butter in a small pan. Add the red pepper flakes and dried mint and briefly heat until fragrant. 12. Drizzle the butter and spice mixture over the soup. Serve hot and enjoy! #ottoman #turkish #soup #EasyRecipes #fyp

🚨 Kaja Kallas: L’Europa deve puntare alla vittoria Il 12 ottobre 2026, l’Alta rappresentante dell’Unione europea per la politica estera, Kaja Kallas, ha chiesto ai Paesi europei di assumere un obiettivo politico chiaro: impedire che la Russia vinca la guerra contro l’Ucraina. Secondo Kallas, cedere alle pressioni di Mosca e accettare concessioni ottenute attraverso l’aggressione rischierebbe di incoraggiare nuove azioni militari in futuro. La responsabile della diplomazia europea ha precisato che spetta agli ucraini stabilire quali condizioni possano rappresentare una vittoria per il loro Paese. La sua dichiarazione non significa quindi che la Russia sia già stata sconfitta militarmente, ma esprime la volontà di orientare la strategia europea verso un risultato che impedisca a Mosca di raggiungere i propri obiettivi attraverso la forza. La posizione di Kallas si inserisce in una strategia che prevede il proseguimento degli aiuti militari e finanziari a Kyiv, il mantenimento delle sanzioni contro la Russia e il rafforzamento della difesa europea. Nella riunione del 12 ottobre, i ministri degli Esteri dell’Ue hanno inoltre discusso nuove misure restrittive contro persone ed entità legate al complesso militare-industriale russo, alla produzione di missili e alle elezioni organizzate da Mosca nei territori ucraini occupati. Kallas ha anche indicato la necessità di contrastare la cosiddetta flotta ombra utilizzata per trasportare petrolio russo e di rendere più efficaci i controlli sulle sanzioni. Parallelamente, l’Unione europea deve affrontare il fabbisogno finanziario dell’Ucraina per il 2027 e valutare un impegno più consistente nel caso in cui il sostegno americano dovesse diminuire. Sul campo, la situazione resta complessa. Tuttavia, non dimostrano che Mosca sia vicina a una sconfitta definitiva. Kyiv continua a dover affrontare carenze di difesa aerea, perdite umane, difficoltà nel reperimento di personale e attacchi alle infrastrutture energetiche. La questione centrale riguarda quindi il futuro della guerra e le condizioni per arrivare a una pace duratura. Per Kallas, l’Europa deve evitare che l’aggressione russa venga premiata con concessioni imposte militarmente.
